note: Labelled claim set for the QA pass in plan §4 (14-17h) and §3 (Taranpreet). Each row states what the pipeline should be able to do with the evidence available to it, not what is true in the world. `scripts/run_test_set.py` runs these and writes data/test_set_results.json with measured outcomes; nothing in this repo quotes an accuracy number that this script did not produce.

fields.expect_direction: the sign of stance_score the run should produce: support | refute | none
fields.expect_verdict: optional exact verdict the run should produce
fields.must_be_decisive: when false, INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE is an acceptable outcome and the row measures only direction

cases.claim: The Eiffel Tower is 330 metres tall.
cases.article: The Eiffel Tower is 330 metres tall. That figure includes the broadcasting antenna added to the tower. A travel brief repeats the height of the Eiffel Tower.
cases.label: supported
cases.why: The corpus sources state the same figure, so evidence should point with the claim.

cases.claim: The Eiffel Tower is 1,000 metres tall.
cases.article: One report claimed the Eiffel Tower is 1,000 metres tall. That number appeared in a hoax thread.
cases.label: refuted
cases.why: Sources give 330 m; a numeric contradiction must be read against the claim, not as agreement.

cases.claim: The Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye.
cases.article: The Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye. An image post repeats that statement as an established fact.
cases.label: refuted-myth
cases.why: The classic myth case: retrieved sources deny it, so direction must be negative.

cases.claim: Vitamin C supplements prevent the common cold in most adults.
cases.article: Vitamin C supplements prevent the common cold in most adults. A retailer made that claim in an advertising campaign.
cases.label: refuted-or-conflicting
cases.why: The corpus contains both the marketing restatement and the fact-check denial; at minimum the refutation must be found.

cases.claim: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
cases.article: A safety leaflet states that lightning never strikes the same place twice. The leaflet was printed in 2009.
cases.label: refuted-myth
cases.why: Tests the polarity rule: a source affirming repeat strikes contradicts a claim phrased with 'never'.

cases.claim: The Empire State Building is struck by lightning about eighty times each year.
cases.article: The Empire State Building is struck by lightning about eighty times each year. A safety leaflet repeats the figure.
cases.label: supported
cases.why: A number the sources carry; agreement should be found without a negation cue.

cases.claim: A consortium has finalised a partnership with the national space agency to build a hydrogen aircraft.
cases.article: A newly formed consortium has finalised a partnership with the national space agency. The consortium will build a hydrogen aircraft by next spring. The announcement came from an account with eleven followers.
cases.label: insufficient
cases.why: Nothing retrievable covers this. The correct output is a non-verdict, not a low-confidence 'false'.

cases.claim: Battery plants are always a poor investment for regional economies.
cases.article: A widely shared travel brief states that the Eiffel Tower is 330 metres tall. Battery plants are always a poor investment for regional economies in my view.
cases.label: opinion
cases.why: An opinion stated in the article must not come back with a stance-bearing verdict.

cases.claim: The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889 for the World's Fair.
cases.article: The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889 for the World's Fair. The tower was completed for the 1889 World's Fair.
cases.label: supported
cases.why: Also checks the invariant that every displayed quote is literally present in the retrieved text.

cases.claim: The company's shares rose 6 percent in after-hours trading on Tuesday.
cases.article: The company's shares rose 6 percent in after-hours trading on Tuesday. The figure was published by the exchange.
cases.label: insufficient
cases.why: A market-moving detail no general source will carry; must degrade to insufficient rather than guess.
